slides.title: Turning browser features off
slides.summary: Permissions-Policy declares which powerful features your page and each iframe may use.
body: Permissions-Policy (formerly Feature-Policy) is a response header that enables or disables browser features such as the camera, microphone, geolocation, payment and fullscreen, for your page and for each iframe.

ul: Least privilege: if your app never uses the camera, turn it off. An XSS payload or third-party script then can't ask for it.
Control embeds: a feature disabled for your page is disabled for every iframe inside it too.
Per-frame grants: the iframe allow attribute delegates a feature to one specific frame.

body: <mark>Disable every powerful feature you don't use, and delegate the rest only to the frames that need them.</mark>

body.text: Feature-Policy was the original name, with a different syntax (camera 'none'). It was renamed Permissions-Policy with structured-header syntax (camera=()). Use the new header; the old one is legacy.

Chromium browsers support the header for many features. Firefox and Safari support the iframe allow attribute but only part of the header, so check each feature on MDN and don't rely on the header alone.

figure.alt: A page at shop.example sends Permissions-Policy: camera=(), geolocation=(self), payment=(self "https://pay.example"). Inside the page, the shop's own code can use geolocation and payment, but not the camera. An iframe from pay.example with allow="payment" can use payment, because the header lists that origin and the attribute delegates it; it cannot use geolocation. An iframe from ads.example gets nothing: no camera, no geolocation, no payment, even if it asks.
